title: What Is Vocation? Work as Calling
excerpt: Vocation is not the job that makes you feel important, it is the place where God hides himself behind your ordinary work to feed your neighbor.
body:
A woman stands at a sink at six in the morning, washing the same dishes she washed last night, and somewhere underneath the steam she is wondering whether any of this counts. She is not lazy. She is not faithless. She has simply absorbed, the way we all absorb the air, a quiet verdict that the real work of God happens somewhere else, in a pulpit or a mission field or a worship band, and that what she does with her two hands at this sink is the part of life you get through so the meaningful part can begin.

I have stood near that sink. I have watched men in my church carry the same suspicion into the cab of a truck, into a classroom, into a cubicle they cannot wait to leave. The question is older than they know, and it is not really a question about jobs. It is a question about whether the eight or ten hours that swallow most of our waking lives have any weight in front of God, or whether they are simply the toll we pay for the privilege of being alive.

The word we reach for is vocation. We have nearly ruined it. In common speech a vocation has become a fancy synonym for a career you happen to enjoy, the work that expresses your inner self, the thing you would do for free if money were no object. That definition sounds generous and it is actually cruel, because it quietly tells the woman at the sink and the man in the truck that they have no vocation at all. Only the lucky few who love their labor get to call it holy. Everyone else is just working.

Let me state the strongest version of the secular objection, because it deserves to be heard plainly. The honest skeptic says this. Calling is a comforting story religion tells to dignify drudgery. There is no cosmic assignment behind your spreadsheet. Work is the exchange of effort for survival, and dressing it in the language of divine purpose is a way of keeping people content with arrangements that mostly serve someone else. He is not entirely wrong. A great deal of vocation talk has functioned exactly that way, a sedative handed to the tired so they will not ask who profits from their tiredness. If your doctrine of work cannot account for the worker who is being ground down, it is not a doctrine. It is propaganda.

So I will not answer the soft version. I will answer that one.

The text I want to carry is the oldest one we have about work, and it falls before anything has gone wrong. 'The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it' (Genesis 2:15 ESV). Read that slowly. The garden is unfallen. There is no curse, no sweat, no thorn. And there is already a job. Before the man is given a wife, before there is a single commandment about good and evil, he is given labor. Work is not the punishment that arrived when paradise broke. Work was in paradise. It is part of what it means to bear the image of a God who himself worked six days and called the result good.

This changes the ground under everything. If work belongs to creation rather than to the fall, then the curse in Genesis 3 did not invent labor, it poisoned labor that already existed. The thorns and the sweat are the corruption of a good thing, not the thing itself. Which means redemption does not rescue us from work. It rescues work.

Martin Luther saw this with a clarity the medieval church had lost. The church of his day had built a two story house. Upstairs lived the priests, the monks, the nuns, the people with a vocatio, a true calling. Downstairs lived the farmer and the cobbler and the mother, doing necessary but spiritually second class things while they waited for Sunday. Luther took an axe to the staircase. He insisted that the milkmaid pouring milk and the monk at prayer stood on level ground before God, that the German word Beruf, calling, belonged to the plowman as fully as to the preacher (Luther). I will treat his argument lightly here, because it has been told elsewhere, but the core of it must stand. There is no hierarchy of holy occupations. There is only faithful and unfaithful labor.

Dorothy Sayers pressed the point into the twentieth century with a sentence that still indicts most of our preaching. She wrote that the church has never quite known what to do with work, that we tell the carpenter not to get drunk and not to cheat his customers, and then we fall silent, when the real Christian question is whether he is making good tables (Sayers 1942). A good table, made well, is not a neutral act that becomes holy only if the carpenter slips a tract into the drawer. The goodness of the table is the worship. God is not impressed by shoddy work done in his name. He is honored by sound work, whether or not the worker can name him yet.

Here is where vocation becomes something other than self expression. Lester DeKoster gave the cleanest definition I have found. Work, he wrote, is the form in which we make ourselves useful to others, and therefore the way we love our neighbor in the most concrete terms available to us (DeKoster 1982). Pull the thread. The farmer does not eat most of what he grows. The nurse does not heal herself. The woman at the sink is feeding people who did not earn the meal. Strip the whole economy down to its bones and you find millions of people serving strangers they will never meet, and the serving is so woven into the ordinary that nobody notices it is love.

Luther had a startling phrase for this. He said that God milks the cows through the milkmaid, that the hands of the laborer are the hands God uses to answer the prayer give us this day our daily bread. You pray for bread. God does not drop loaves from the sky. He feeds you through a farmer, a miller, a baker, a trucker, a clerk, a chain of human hands most of whom have no idea they are participating in an answered prayer. Vocation is the mask of God. He hides behind your ordinary work and uses it to keep his world alive.

Now return to the skeptic, who was right that calling has been used as a sedative. He was right, and the answer is not to abandon vocation but to recover the half of it the sedative left out. Because if my work is genuinely the place where God loves my neighbor through my hands, then any arrangement that crushes the worker or empties the work of its service is not a neutral economic fact. It is a violation of something sacred. The doctrine that dignifies the laborer is the same doctrine that condemns his exploitation. You cannot hold one without the other. The factory that treats a man as a disposable input is not merely inefficient. It is desecrating an image bearer at the exact point where he was made to reflect God most clearly.

Studs Terkel spent years recording how Americans actually talk about their jobs, and the ache that runs through his pages is not that the work is hard. It is that the work feels meaningless, that people suspect they are interchangeable, that nobody would notice if they vanished (Terkel 1974). That ache is theological before it is economic. It is the cry of people made for vocation and handed only employment.

So what is vocation. It is not the career that flatters you. It is not the passion you would chase if the bills disappeared. It is the ordinary labor, paid or unpaid, glamorous or invisible, through which God serves your neighbor while wearing you as his mask. The woman at the sink is not waiting for her real calling. Her hands are full of it. The dishes she is washing will hold the food that feeds the people God gave her, and the steam rising off the water is closer to incense than she has been told.

The man who wants only to feel important will never see this, because importance is exactly the wrong measure. The kingdom does not run on importance. It runs on service that mostly goes unwatched. And the test of whether you have understood your vocation is not whether it makes you feel significant. It is whether, when you set down your tools tonight, someone you may never meet was quietly fed.

That is the calling. It was here before the fall. It will outlast your ambition.

### Works Cited

DeKoster, Lester. Work the Meaning of Your Life. Grand Rapids: Christian's Library Press, 1982.

Luther, Martin. The Estate of Marriage and selected writings on vocation. In Luther's Works. Philadelphia: Fortress Press.

Sayers, Dorothy L. Why Work? London: Methuen, 1942.

Terkel, Studs. Working. New York: Pantheon Books, 1974.

title: How to Find God's Will for Your Career
excerpt: God is far less concerned with the one perfect job he has hidden from you than with the kind of person you are becoming in whatever work you already hold.
body:
A young man sat across from me in my office and asked the question I have heard in some form a hundred times. He had two job offers. He had prayed about both. And he was terrified, not of choosing wrong in the ordinary way, but of missing the one path God had ordained, as if there were a single correct door and a hundred wrong ones, and the whole weight of his future rested on his ability to read a sign God had so far declined to send. He was not asking how to be faithful. He was asking how to crack a code.

I know that fear from the inside. I came to faith out of atheism, and one of the strange aftereffects of conversion is that you can carry your old habits of mind into your new life without noticing. The atheist in me had believed the universe was indifferent and silent. The new convert sometimes flipped that into its anxious opposite, a universe so loaded with hidden divine signals that every decision became a minefield. Both are forms of fear. Both put the burden in the wrong place.

The question people are really asking when they ask how to find God's will for their career is this. Is there a specific job, company, or city that God has chosen for me, and will he be displeased if I fail to discover it. And underneath that question sits an assumption so common we rarely examine it, the assumption that God's will is mostly a matter of hidden information, a treasure map he has drawn and then hidden, and that the spiritual life is largely the work of finding what he has concealed.

Let me give the strongest version of the opposing instinct, the one held by sincere and serious Christians, because I held it myself and it is not foolish. The argument runs this way. God is sovereign over every detail of my life. He numbers the hairs on my head and the days of my years. Surely a God that attentive has an opinion about something as consequential as my career, and surely the loving thing is for him to communicate it, so that the faithful response is to wait, to seek, to keep asking until the specific answer comes. There is real truth in this. God is sovereign over the details. He does direct. The book of Acts is full of doors opened and closed, of the Spirit forbidding Paul to go one direction and compelling him another. To deny that God guides would be to deny the whole testimony of Scripture.

So I will not deny it. I will say that the people who hold this view have mistaken the exception for the rule, and have built a whole anxious method out of moments God reserved for himself.

The text I want to carry is short and it has been worn smooth by overuse, which is a shame, because read in context it cuts the legs out from under the entire treasure map. 'This is the will of God, your sanctification' (1 Thessalonians 4:3 ESV). Paul is writing to people who, like us, surely had questions about their work, their marriages, their futures in a hostile city. And when he names the will of God explicitly, he does not say a location. He does not say an occupation. He says sanctification. The thing God most certainly wills for you is not a job. It is a kind of person. He wills that you become holy, truthful, sexually faithful, hardworking, dependent on him, useful to your neighbor. That will is not hidden. It fills the New Testament. And it is the will that most of us are quietly avoiding while we agonize over the will he never promised to spell out.

This reframes the whole search. The decisive question is not which of these two jobs is the secret correct one. The decisive question is which of these two jobs will let me become the person God has clearly said he wants me to be, and in which can I most fully serve the people he puts in front of me. Those are answerable questions. They involve wisdom, counsel, honest self knowledge, the shape of your gifts, the needs of your family, the welfare of your neighbor. They do not require a sign. They require sanctified common sense, which God has been forming in you the whole time.

The revolt of the conscience against a buried clergy class. Luther again, lightly, because his point bears directly here. When the Reformation flattened the staircase between sacred and secular work, it also demolished the idea that only special people receive special callings. The plowman did not need a vision to know his plowing was holy. He needed to plow well, in faith, for his neighbor. I mention Luther only to say this. The treasure map theory of career guidance is a quiet return to the very hierarchy the Reformation broke, the notion that the truly spiritual receive direct downloads while ordinary believers stumble in the dark. The biblical picture is humbler and far more freeing. God has given you his revealed will, your sanctification, a renewed mind, wise counsel, and a brain. That is the equipment. Use it.

The treasure map anxiety also has a more recent and datable history, and seeing it helps loosen its grip. Two streams fed it. The first was secular. When Frank Parsons opened the first vocation bureau in Boston in 1908 and his Choosing a Vocation appeared the next year, a whole apparatus was born around the conviction that for each person there is a right occupational match waiting to be scientifically discovered, and that the great danger is choosing wrong. That picture seeped into the water everyone drinks. The second stream was inside the church. By the middle of the twentieth century a particular evangelical piety had hardened into what its critics named the traditional view, the belief that God has an individual blueprint for each believer, a single ideal career and spouse and city, which the faithful must discern or else fall to second best. Garry Friesen gave that view its name and its sharpest challenge in 1980, arguing that Scripture nowhere promises such a hidden personal blueprint and that the search for it had become a tyranny dressed as devotion (Friesen 1980). The young man in my office was not inventing his fear. He had inherited it, from a vocational science a century old and a piety almost as old, both of which told him that somewhere there was one right answer and that missing it was the thing to dread.

Dallas Willard put it with characteristic steadiness. He warned against treating guidance as a kind of magic, a bypass around the slow work of becoming wise, and he insisted that God's preferred method of leading mature people is through their renewed character and sound judgment, not through a perpetual stream of supernatural memos (Willard 1984). A father does not leave detailed instructions for a grown son on how to tie his shoes. The maturity is the guidance. If you must hear an audible voice before every ordinary decision, that is not deeper faith. It is arrested development dressed as piety.

Tim Keller and Katherine Leary Alsdorf, writing for people in demanding careers, made a related and bracing observation. Much of our paralysis over God's will, they argued, is not really spiritual at all. It is the fear of limitation, the refusal to accept that choosing one good thing means losing another, the secret hope that somewhere there is an option with no cost (Keller and Alsdorf 2012). We baptize that fear and call it seeking God's will, when what we are actually seeking is a guarantee against regret. There is no such guarantee. To take a job is to close a door. To marry is to forsake all others. The cross does its work right here, in the death of the fantasy that you can have the whole field of possibility forever. Faithfulness means choosing, and trusting God to redeem what the choosing costs.

Now let the law fall before the grace, because it must. The honest truth is that most of our career anxiety is not humility before God. It is the desire to be exceptional. We want our work to be remarkable, our path to be singular, our lives to matter in a way the neighbor's life does not. The frantic search for a custom divine plan is often pride wearing the costume of devotion. I have done this. I have wanted God to confirm that I was special before I would consent to be faithful. That is the sin under the searching, and naming it is the first mercy.

The grace is this. You are released. The God who wills your sanctification is not standing over you with a hidden answer key, scoring your ability to guess. He has already told you the main thing. Become like Christ. Serve your neighbor. Work honestly. Provide for those depending on you. Within that, you are astonishingly free. Take the job that lets you do those things. If two jobs both let you do them, take either one, and trust that a sovereign God can write straight with the line you chose. Wendell Berry, who has thought as hard as anyone about staying put and doing good work in one place, noticed that the people most at peace with their labor are usually not the ones who found a perfect calling but the ones who accepted a real place and gave themselves to it (Berry 1990). The faithfulness is in the giving, not in the finding.

So here is how to find God's will for your career. Stop hunting for the version he hid. Pick up the version he revealed. Pursue the holiness he commanded. Get counsel from people who love you and will tell you the truth. Weigh your gifts against your neighbor's needs. Then choose, and walk through the door, and labor at what lies in front of you so well that God is honored by the doing.

The young man in my office wanted me to tell him which offer was the right one. I could not, and I would not if I could, because the answer he needed was larger than the question he asked. The job was never the point. He was.

### Works Cited

Berry, Wendell. What Are People For? San Francisco: North Point Press, 1990.

Friesen, Garry. Decision Making and the Will of God: A Biblical Alternative to the Traditional View. Portland: Multnomah Press, 1980.

Keller, Timothy, and Katherine Leary Alsdorf. Every Good Endeavor. New York: Dutton, 2012.

Parsons, Frank. Choosing a Vocation. Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1909.

Willard, Dallas. In Search of Guidance. Ventura: Regal Books, 1984.

title: A Christian View of Personal Finance
excerpt: The question is never simply how to manage your money well, it is whether your money is managing you, because Jesus treated wealth as a rival god and not a neutral tool.
body:
A man told me once, with real relief in his voice, that he had finally gotten his finances under control. He had a budget. He had an emergency fund. He had a retirement plan with a number at the end of it that let him sleep. And as I listened I felt something I could not name at first, a kind of unease underneath my genuine gladness for him, because everything he described was wise and good and I would counsel any person in my church to do the same, and yet the whole picture had quietly rearranged itself around a center that was not God. He had not bought a single foolish thing. He had simply built a fortress, and the fortress had a name, and the name was security.

I know that fortress. I was raised without a father, which among other things means I was raised with a certain low grade financial fear that never fully leaves a person. When you grow up watching a household do math at the kitchen table that does not work, money stops being neutral very early. It becomes the thing standing between you and the abyss. So when I talk about money as a rival god, I am not preaching down at anyone. I am describing the inside of my own chest.

Most Christian personal finance advice is true and incomplete in the same way the man's fortress was true and incomplete. Spend less than you earn. Avoid debt that enslaves you. Save. Give. Invest patiently. All of it is sound. None of it is wrong. And almost all of it operates on an assumption it never examines, the assumption that money is a tool, morally neutral, and the only question is whether you wield it skillfully. That assumption is exactly where I want to push, because it is not what Jesus said.

Let me give the strongest version of the neutral tool view, because serious Christians hold it and it is not stupid. Money, the argument goes, is simply stored labor, a medium of exchange, no more moral than a hammer. A hammer can build a house or break a skull. Money can fund a hospital or a brothel. The morality lives in the user, not the instrument, and therefore the Christian task is competent stewardship, learning to use the neutral tool for good ends. There is real truth here. Scripture does call us stewards. It does praise the servant who invested wisely and rebuke the one who buried his talent in fear. Proverbs is full of practical financial wisdom that assumes money can serve righteous ends. To despise money as inherently evil is a heresy the Bible does not teach.

So I grant the tool. And then I notice that Jesus refused to leave it a tool.

The text I want to carry is one sentence, and it should unsettle anyone who has reduced money to a hammer. 'No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money' (Matthew 6:24 ESV). Hear what Jesus does in that sentence. He does not say you cannot serve God while owning a hammer. He does not set up God against carpentry. He sets up God against money, as a master against a master, as a god against a God. The word he uses, mammon, is not the cash in your pocket. It is the spirit behind the cash, the power that promises what only God can give, security, identity, freedom from fear, and then demands your worship in return. Jesus did not treat money as neutral. He treated it as a personality, a rival deity with a claim on the human heart.

This is the hinge that most financial teaching slides right past. The danger is not that you will use the tool badly. The danger is that the tool will use you, that it will quietly migrate from your hand to your throne, and that you will not notice the coronation because nothing about it looks like idolatry. The man with the fortress was not greedy. He gave generously. He did not worship money the way a miser does. He worshiped it the way an anxious person does, by trusting it to do for him what he could not bring himself to trust God to do. There is a worship of accumulation and there is a worship of security, and the second is far more respectable and just as deadly.

Here the historical root matters, and it cuts against us. The Protestant world inherited a powerful engine for producing wealth, the conviction that diligent labor in one's calling honored God, that thrift was a virtue and waste a sin. Max Weber traced how that conviction, sincere and pious in the beginning, gradually shed its theology and kept its habits, leaving behind a culture that worked hard and saved hard and accumulated steadily while forgetting why (Weber 1905). I treat Weber lightly, because the story has been told, but the warning lands directly on Christian personal finance. The same impulse that makes us responsible can make us idolatrous, and the line between stewardship and the fortress is almost invisible from the inside. The diligent saver and the trusting believer can look identical for years, until a loss comes and reveals which master they were actually serving.

Wendell Berry saw the cultural version of this and named it with quiet force. A society that measures everything by accumulation, he observed, will eventually treat people and land and time the way it treats money, as inputs to be optimized, and will lose the capacity to recognize the goods that cannot be counted (Berry 1990). The household that runs purely on the logic of net worth will eventually run its relationships that way too. Children become expenses. Sabbath becomes inefficiency. The neighbor becomes either a customer or an obstacle. The tool, left on the throne, reshapes everything in its own flat image.

Now let the law fall, because a Christian view of personal finance has to pass through judgment before it reaches comfort. Examine where your security actually lives. Not what you say in church. What your stomach does when the account drops. What you reach for when the fear comes at three in the morning. For many of us, and I include myself, the honest answer is that we trust the number more than we trust the Lord, that our peace rises and falls with the balance, and that this is not stewardship. It is functional atheism with a budget. The tithe does not fix this. You can give ten percent and still serve mammon with the ninety. The question is not the percentage. The question is the throne.

And now the grace, which is the only thing that actually frees the hand to give. The reason the Christian can hold money loosely is not that money does not matter. It is that the account has already been settled somewhere else. 'You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich' (2 Corinthians 8:9 ESV). The richest being in existence emptied himself, took on poverty, went to a cross with nothing, and in doing so secured for you a wealth that no market can touch and no loss can reach. That is the ground on which generosity becomes possible. You do not give in order to be secure. You give because you already are.

So a Christian view of personal finance keeps every practical thing the world's wisdom got right. Budget. Save. Avoid the debt that enslaves. Provide for your household, which Scripture treats as a non negotiable duty. But it sets all of it under a single ruthless question, the one Jesus forces. Who is the master. If money is your servant, use it skillfully and give it away freely. If money is your master, no amount of skill will save you, because you do not have a budgeting problem. You have a worship problem.

The man with the fortress was not wrong to build it. He was wrong to live in it. The walls he raised against fear had become the walls that kept God at a manageable distance, and the security he gained was the exact thing he would have to lose to be free.

Not a tool. A master, asking for your soul.

### Works Cited

Berry, Wendell. What Are People For? San Francisco: North Point Press, 1990.

Weber, Max. The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. 1905. Translated by Talcott Parsons, London: Allen and Unwin, 1930.

Keller, Timothy. Counterfeit Gods. New York: Dutton, 2009.

title: Rest, Ambition, and the Idol of Success
excerpt: Ambition is not the disease and rest is not the cure, the real question is whose voice you are working to silence and whether you can stop long enough to find out.
body:
A pastor I respect ran himself into the ground and called it faithfulness. He worked the hours, took the meetings, answered the midnight calls, skipped the vacations, and when his body finally failed him he was genuinely surprised, because he had spent years treating exhaustion as evidence of devotion. He was not lazy and he was not vain in any way the church would recognize. He was the opposite of the prosperity preacher chasing a private jet. And he was just as enslaved, to a god the church almost never names because it wears the robes of virtue.

I watched him with a particular dread, because I saw myself. I run hot. I always have. Some of it is gift and some of it is wound, and I have spent a long time unable to tell the two apart. A man raised without a father often learns early that he must produce his own worth, that no one is going to hand him a name, that he will be exactly as valuable as his last accomplishment. That lesson does not leave when you become a Christian. It just learns to quote Scripture. It tells you that your relentlessness is stewardship, that your inability to stop is a high view of the work, that the tiredness in your bones is the cost of caring more than other people.

So I want to be careful, because the easy sermon here is the wrong one. The easy sermon says ambition is bad and rest is good, that the driven need to slow down and the slow down is the gospel. That sermon is shallow and it is not even true. The real question underneath rest and ambition and success is not how much you are working. It is who you are working for, and whose verdict you are trying to earn, and whether you could survive the silence of stopping long enough to find out.

Let me give the strongest case for ambition, because the church too often slanders it. The serious objection runs this way. Ambition is the engine of every good thing humans have built. The cathedral, the cure, the symphony, the rescued child, the business that employs a hundred families, none of it came from people content to coast. Scripture itself praises the diligent and rebukes the sluggard. Paul drove himself harder than almost anyone in history, working with his hands by night and preaching by day, pressing on toward the goal, running to win. To make rest the highest virtue is to baptize sloth and call laziness holy. There is real truth in this, and the contemplative wing of the church needs to hear it. God is a worker. He made an industrious world and called industry good. The problem with the burned out pastor was never that he aimed high.

So I grant the engine. And then I ask what fuel it was burning.

The text I want to carry is the oldest law about stopping, and it is stranger than we let it be. 'Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God. On it you shall not do any work' (Exodus 20:8-10 ESV). Notice what kind of command this is. It is not a suggestion for the tired. It is law, carved in stone, set among the prohibitions on murder and theft and adultery. God treated the refusal to rest as belonging in the same list as those. And notice who it covers. The servant, the foreigner, the ox. Sabbath was the one law that made it illegal to work people without limit, the one place where the relentless logic of production was forced to halt. The God who worked six days stopped on the seventh, not from fatigue, but to declare that the world did not depend on his ceaseless labor, and to teach his people that it did not depend on theirs.

This is the hinge. Sabbath is not primarily about rest as recovery, the way we use a weekend to recharge for more work. Sabbath is a weekly confession that you are not God, that the world will keep turning while you sleep, that your striving is not what holds the universe together. To stop is to preach a sermon with your body, a sermon that says the Lord reigns and I do not have to. Which is precisely why the ambitious cannot do it. Stopping exposes the lie they are living by, the lie that everything depends on them, and so they keep moving partly because motion lets them avoid the verdict that waits in the stillness.

The historical root here runs straight through the Protestant inheritance, and it indicts us. The same tradition that recovered the dignity of work, that taught the plowman his labor was holy, gradually let that good teaching curdle. Max Weber watched the doctrine of the calling, sincere at the start, harden into a culture where ceaseless productivity became a sign of being chosen, where the inability to rest looked like proof of grace rather than its absence (Weber 1905). I touch Weber lightly because his story has been told, but the line he traced ends in the burned out pastor's office. We took the holiness of work and quietly dropped the holiness of stopping. We kept the six days and lost the seventh. And we built a Christianity that can preach Sabbath beautifully while making it functionally impossible to practice, because the whole apparatus runs on people who will not stop.

Dorothy Sayers, who loved good work fiercely, still saw the trap. The point of work, she insisted, is the excellence of the thing made, not the importance it confers on the maker, and the moment work becomes a way of proving your worth rather than serving your neighbor, it has been corrupted at the root (Sayers 1942). That is the precise corruption the idol of success performs. It takes the good thing, useful labor, and bends it into a mirror, so that you are no longer working to make a good table but to become a person of consequence, no longer serving the neighbor but auditioning for a verdict. And the audition never ends, because the idol never says enough.

Let the law fall now, and let it fall on the respectable. The driven among us, and I am one, must hear that our relentlessness is often not virtue but unbelief. We cannot stop because we do not trust the verdict already spoken over us, and so we keep trying to speak a better one with our output. That is idolatry, the worship of a success that promises to tell us we are finally enough and never does. It is no holier than the prosperity preacher's greed. It is the same hunger wearing a more flattering suit. The burned out pastor did not collapse because he loved God too much. He collapsed because, somewhere underneath the service, he was still working to earn a name his Father had already given him for free.

And here, finally, the grace, which is the only thing strong enough to let a driven man stop. The reason you can rest is that the decisive work is finished, and it is not yours. 'It is finished' (John 19:30 ESV). On the cross the one work that actually held the universe together was completed, and you were not the one who completed it. Your name was secured by his labor, not yours. Which means you can lay your tools down, not because the work does not matter, but because your worth no longer rides on it. The ambition can stay, redeemed, pointed now at the neighbor's good instead of your own verdict. The rest can come, not as collapse, but as confession. He reigns. You do not have to.

So rest is not the cure for ambition and ambition is not the disease. The disease is the idol of success, the god who feeds on your striving and never grants the peace it promises. Kill that god, and your ambition is freed to build good things for the right reason. Kill that god, and Sabbath stops being a threat and becomes a homecoming.

The pastor who ran himself into the ground is recovering now, slowly, learning the hardest lesson the driven ever learn. That the world held together while he rested. That it always would have. That it never needed his exhaustion, and neither did God.

### Works Cited

Sayers, Dorothy L. Why Work? London: Methuen, 1942.

Weber, Max. The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. 1905. Translated by Talcott Parsons, London: Allen and Unwin, 1930.

Peterson, Eugene H. The Contemplative Pastor. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1989.

title: Bivocational Ministry Done Right
excerpt: The pastor who works a second job is not a half pastor settling for less, he stands in the oldest and most honest tradition of Christian ministry, with dirt still under his fingernails.
body:
A man called me late on a Tuesday, ashamed in a way he could barely put into words. He pastored a small church in a small town, forty people on a good Sunday, and to feed his family he drove a delivery route four days a week. He had spent the afternoon at a denominational gathering listening to talk of growth strategies and full time placements and church health metrics, and he had come away convinced he was a failure, a man who could not make ministry work and had to prop it up with a real job. He used those words. A real job. As if the route were the embarrassment and the pulpit were the dream that had not quite come true.

I wanted to reach through the phone. Because I have stood near that shame, and because the verdict he had absorbed is not just discouraging, it is a lie with a long history, and the lie has done real damage to real men who deserved better from the church that formed them.

The term we use is bivocational, a pastor who holds paid work outside the church alongside his ministry. The word itself reveals the problem. We call it bivocational as if the second job were a separate vocation grudgingly added on, a compromise, a sign that the church could not afford to do the thing properly. The assumption buried in our language is that the normal, mature, successful pastor is fully funded by the congregation, free of secular labor, devoted entirely to the work of ministry, and that the man on the delivery route is a developmental stage on the way to that ideal, or worse, a man who never got there.

Let me state the strongest case for full time, salaried ministry, because it is a serious case and I am not interested in romanticizing poverty. The argument runs this way. The laborer deserves his wages. Paul himself wrote that those who preach the gospel should get their living by the gospel, that the elder who labors in preaching and teaching is worthy of double honor, including financial honor. A pastor pulled in two directions cannot give the church his full attention. Study suffers. Visitation suffers. The man is exhausted. A congregation that truly valued its shepherd would free him to shepherd, and the drive toward full time support is therefore not worldliness but love. There is genuine truth in this. Scripture does defend the right of ministers to be paid, and a church that could support its pastor and refuses to, out of stinginess, is sinning against him. I will not pretend otherwise.

So I grant the wages. And then I notice who wrote the verse about them.

The text I want to carry is Paul describing his own practice, and it should end the shame on the delivery route forever. 'You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak' (Acts 20:34-35 ESV). The man who wrote that ministers deserve their wages chose, repeatedly, not to take them. He made tents. He worked with his hands, by his own account often into exhaustion, so that the gospel would cost his hearers nothing and so that no one could accuse him of preaching for profit. The greatest missionary in the history of the church was, by our anxious modern definition, bivocational. The dirt under his fingernails was not a failure of fundraising. It was a deliberate strategy, and he held it up as an example to follow.

This is the reversal the ashamed pastor needs. Bivocational ministry is not a fallback from the New Testament model. In significant part it is the New Testament model. The fully salaried, professionally credentialed, vocationally segregated pastor is the historical novelty, not the bivocational tentmaker. For most of the church's life, in most of the world even now, the man who preaches on Sunday works alongside his people the rest of the week, and that arrangement was not a defect to be outgrown. It was a witness. It put the pastor inside the same economic weather as his congregation, subject to the same bosses and deadlines and money fears, and it made his preaching about work and money and ambition something other than theory.

The historical root here is worth naming with care, because the Reformation cuts both ways on this question. When Luther flattened the staircase between sacred and secular labor, he did something we have only half received. He declared that the cobbler and the preacher stood on level ground before God, that there was no holy class of work and no profane class. I treat this lightly, because the larger story has been told, but follow what it means for the man on the delivery route. If Luther was right, then the delivery route is not the unholy half of his week that subsidizes the holy half. The route is itself ministry, holy labor, the love of neighbor through useful work, no less sacred than the sermon. The bivocational pastor is not a man living half in the sacred and half in the secular. He is a man for whom Luther's insight has become his actual life, because he cannot afford the illusion that the two are separable.

Lester DeKoster would push it further. Work, he argued, is the form love takes when it becomes useful to a neighbor, and the worker who serves people through honest labor is doing exactly what the worker was made to do (DeKoster 1982). The pastor delivering packages is loving the people on his route in the most concrete way available, putting bread on tables, keeping the small machinery of a community running, and then standing up on Sunday to preach to people who know he understands their week because he has lived it. That is not a diluted ministry. In certain ways it is a more credible one. The skeptic in the pew who suspects the clergy of living off other people's labor has no such suspicion of the man who clocks in beside him on Monday.

Now let the law fall, because it must fall on the church, not on the bivocational pastor. The shame that man carried was put on him. It was manufactured by a church culture that measures success by salary and staff size, that treats the small congregation as a problem to be solved rather than a flock to be loved, that has so absorbed the metrics of the corporation that it can no longer see the tentmaker as anything but a man who failed to scale. That is our sin, and I include myself in it, because I have admired the wrong things and praised the wrong men and made the faithful pastor of forty people feel like a footnote. We did this to him. The repentance belongs to us.

And here the grace, which is the same grace that funded Paul's tents. The pastor's worth was never going to come from his salary or his attendance or his place in the denominational hierarchy. It was secured at a cross, by a carpenter, a man who worked with his hands for thirty years before he preached a word, who knew the smell of sawdust and the ache of labor and chose to enter the world through a workshop rather than a palace. The Lord the bivocational pastor serves was himself, by every measure his denomination would apply, a working man. There is no shame in the route, because there was no shame in the carpenter's shop.

So bivocational ministry done right is not full time ministry with an asterisk. It is ministry in the line of Paul and in the shadow of the carpenter, a pastor who has refused to let his calling float free of the economic weather his people live in, who preaches about work with his own hands still sore from it. Done right, it asks the congregation to honor the man and support him as they are able, because the laborer does deserve his wages. And done right, it refuses the lie that the man who cannot yet be paid in full is anything less than a real pastor with a real calling.

The man on the delivery route hung up that night a little steadier. He is still driving. He is still preaching. And the next time someone asks him when he is going to get a real job, I hope he remembers that the realest pastor who ever lived made tents, and the realest one of all made tables.

Luther, Martin. Selected writings on vocation and the priesthood of all believers. In Luther's Works. Philadelphia: Fortress Press.
